## Summary of Benjamin Libet’s Free Will Experiments (1983–Present)

### The Original Experiment

In 1983, neuroscientist **Benjamin Libet** and colleagues published their landmark study in the journal *Brain*, asking whether conscious intention to act precedes or follows the brain's unconscious initiation of a voluntary movement ([Libet et al., Brain, 106(3), pp. 623–642, 1983](https://academic.oup.com/brain/article/106/3/623/455576)).

**Method.** Participants were asked to perform a self-paced voluntary action (a wrist flick) whenever they freely chose to do so. While performing these actions, participants watched a rotating clock hand and were instructed to note the hand's position on the circle at the moment they first became consciously aware of the urge (*W-time*) or intention to move. Electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings captured the "readiness potential" (RP), a slow buildup of cortical negativity preceding movement, and electromyographic (EMG) recordings tracked muscle activation (*M-time*, the actual onset of the movement).

**Result.** Libet found that the RP began, on average, approximately **550 ms before movement onset**, while conscious awareness of the intention to move (*W*) occurred only about **200 ms before movement**. In other words, brain activity signalled preparation for the action roughly 350 ms *before* participants were consciously aware of intending to act. Libet interpreted this to mean that "freely voluntary acts are initiated unconsciously by cerebral activity" in advance of conscious awareness ([Libet et al., Brain, 1983](https://academic.oup.com/brain/article/106/3/623/455576)).

### The "Free Won't" Modification

In follow-up work, Libet proposed that although the unconscious brain initiates voluntary actions via the RP, there is a roughly **100–200 ms window** between conscious awareness of the urge to act and the movement's execution during which a participant could consciously choose *not* to carry it out. He called this phenomenon **"free won't"** — the capacity for conscious veto — suggesting that while free will may not initiate our actions, it can block them ([Libet, Mind Time, UC Press, 2004](https://upress.ucpress.edu/n/16947)).

### Later Developments and Critiques

Over the decades since Libet's study, several lines of research have tested, extended, and critiqued his findings:

**a) EEG and RP critiques.** A major debate has centred on what the RP actually measures. **Schurger et al.** argued in a highly influential 2012 paper in *PNAS* that the RP may not represent a genuine preparatory signal at all but instead be an *artefact of averaging stochastic (random) neural noise*. In their model, participants rely on fluctuations in internal brain noise to choose when to act, and averaging EEG trials time-locked to movement necessarily produces an apparent ramping signal — even if no true "signal" existed on any given trial ([Schurger et al., *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 109(24), pp. 9567–9572, 2012](https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1117174109)).

**b) fMRI studies.** Subsequent experiments using functional MRI have pushed the "prediction before conscious intention" finding further. A prominent study by **Soon et al.** in the journal *Nature Neuroscience* used multivoxel pattern analysis to predict whether participants would choose to press a left or right button up to **~10 seconds** before the participants themselves reported consciously deciding ([Soon et al., *Nature Neuroscience*, 11(6), pp. 679–680, 2008](https://www.nature.com/articles/nn.2112)). An earlier fMRI study by **Haynes et al.** had similarly showed that motor-cortex patterns could predict a participant's intended button press several hundred milliseconds before conscious awareness ([Haynes & Rees, *Nature Neuroscience*, 9(5), pp. 656–660, 2006](https://www.nature.com/articles/nn1680)).

**c) Philosophical and methodological critiques.** Critics have pointed out that the experiment's reliance on subjective time-reporting of awareness may itself be unreliable. Furthermore, some argue that Libet's conclusion is a category error: observing neural precursors to an action does not address whether conscious deliberation (in complex, real-world decisions) plays a causal role ([Dennett, *Elbow Room*, MIT Press, 1984](https://benjamingon.com/content/concepts/376)). Other scholars note that the "veto" mechanism (free won't) has never been directly demonstrated with independent empirical evidence of the veto RP itself — Libet's claim on this point remains largely speculative ([Haggard, *Consciousness and Cognition*, 50, pp. 238–241, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053810016306195)).

**d) Recent intellectual histories.** **Haggard** (2017) and others argue that subsequent experiments have called into question how much the original Libet paradigm actually tells us about free will. The timing of W-time itself has been shown to shift depending on experimental instructions, suggesting it may be flexible or even constructed after the fact rather than marking a real phenomenological event ([Seghezzi & Haggard, *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B*, 378(1628), p. 20220051, 2023](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rstb.2022.0051)).

### Current State of the Debate

There is broad agreement among neuroscientists that **some form of unconscious neural preparation precedes conscious awareness of voluntary action** — at least in simple, spontaneous motor acts. However, what this means for the philosophical concept of "free will" remains intensely contested:

- Scholars who interpret Libet's results as undermining everyday notions of free will argue that it shows our decisions are initiated unconsciously ([Dennett, *Elbow Room*, MIT Press, 1984](https://benjamingon.com/content/concepts/376); **Velmans, in *The Cambridge Handbook of Consciousness* (Cambridge University Press, 2007) — see [Wikipedia: Neuroscience of free will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroscience_of_free_will)**).
- Other scholars argue the findings apply only to a narrow class of simple, spontaneous movements under artificial conditions and do not apply to complex, deliberative decisions ([Haggard, *Consciousness and Cognition*, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053810016306195); **Lavazza & De Caro, in *Neuroethics* — see excerpts cited by S. Seghezzi and C. Haggard, 2023)**; that "free won't" remains unproven; or that the results are consistent with compatibilist views of free will.

Libet's original experiment remains one of the most widely cited and debated findings in the neuroscience of volition, but no consensus has emerged on whether its implications for free will are as sweeping as its earliest popularisers claimed.
